paper.title: In-context learning predicts clinical endpoints from bulk transcriptomes across diseases and platforms
paper.abstract: Bulk transcriptomes carry information on diagnosis, treatment response and survival, but clinical cohorts are small, and each gets a model of its own that often fails in the next cohort. Here we present PRTS, a 220-million-parameter model that reads a labelled cohort as context and predicts binary, multiclass, continuous or survival endpoints for new samples from whole transcriptomes, without per-cohort training. PRTS was pretrained on 6.0 million tasks generated from public RNA-seq profiles. On 175 held-out tasks and 44 tasks from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), it had the highest mean predictive accuracy, narrowly ahead of TabPFN v3.5, the strongest pre-specified comparator. The lead came from within-cohort prediction and, on TCGA, mainly from survival tasks; across cohorts and at unseen sites, PRTS was level with the strongest tabular models while running more than twice as fast as TabPFN v3.5. The same weights transfer labels to new cohorts from public references, forecast accuracy from pilots, flag suspect labels and attribute predictions to genes. We release the prior, the pretraining code and the model with its weights, together with RealBulk, a collection of 1,160 curated public cohorts, and its benchmark.
paper.tldr: A 220M-parameter model pretrained on 6M public RNA-seq tasks reads a labeled cohort as context and predicts binary, multiclass, continuous, or survival endpoints for new whole-transcriptome samples without per-cohort training, achieving the best average accuracy on 219 held-out tasks while transferring labels, forecasting accuracy, and flagging suspect labels.
paper.why: PRTS is a genuinely new capability: a single in-context-learning model that handles diagnosis, survival, and regression endpoints across diseases and platforms without per-cohort retraining, backed by 6M pretraining tasks, a 175-task benchmark, and open weights plus a 1,160-cohort resource. It beats strong tabular baselines and transfers labels across cohorts, which could change how bulk transcriptomic prediction is done in practice. Its generality across tasks, cohorts, and endpoints exceeds the other strong candidates.

summary.tldr: PRTS is a 220M-parameter transformer that performs in-context prediction of binary, multiclass, continuous, and censored survival endpoints from whole bulk transcriptomes with no per-cohort training, slightly outperforming TabPFN v3.5 on held-out benchmarks while running 2.6x faster.
summary.background: Bulk transcriptomes predict diagnosis, response, and survival, but clinical cohorts are small (median 107 people) and models fitted per cohort fail to transfer across cohorts, platforms, and sites. Existing foundation models either need per-endpoint fine-tuning (transcriptomic models like Geneformer) or are designed for narrow tables without survival handling (TabPFN), and cross-cohort distribution shift remains unsolved.
summary.approach: The authors built PRTS (Prior-trained RNA-seq Task Solver), pretrained on 6.0M anonymized tasks generated by a prior from 581,503 public RNA-seq profiles (PreBULK, 20,010 genes); genes enter as random codes so no gene identity is learned, and attention along genes through inducing tokens gives linear cost over full transcriptomes. It was evaluated against 13 pre-specified comparators (plus post hoc TabPFN v3.5 configurations) on 175 held-out tasks from 174 held-out RealBulk cohorts and 44 tasks from 13 TCGA projects, scored by rank correlation (2xAUC-1 for binary, 2xC-1 for survival). The same weights support four applications: label transfer from reference cohorts (Hub), accuracy forecasting from 30-person pilots (Planner), label-error auditing, and integrated-gradient gene attribution.
findings: PRTS achieved the highest mean rank correlation on both benchmarks (0.376 on RealBulk, +0.013 over TabPFN v3.5, Holm-adjusted p=0.016; 0.385 on TCGA, +0.019), but the margin is narrow.

The lead came mainly from within-cohort prediction (+0.018 over TabPFN v3.5) and TCGA survival tasks (+0.038); across cohorts and at unseen sites it was level with TabPFN v3.5 (+0.008 and +0.007, intervals including zero).
Leads over post hoc TabPFN v3.5 configurations (6,000 genes, or SurvivalTabPFN for survival) on RealBulk did not survive Holm adjustment (p=0.054 and 0.059).
PRTS ran 2.6x faster than TabPFN v3.5 (37.5 vs 96.6 s per 1,000 samples on RealBulk) and had the best integrated Brier skill score for survival (0.081 RealBulk, 0.069 TCGA).

Applications: multi-reference label transfer (Hub) beat SingleR-style transfer by +0.059 but was level with TabPFN v3.5 given the same references; Planner forecast full-study accuracy from pilots with MAE 0.180 vs 0.260 for least-squares extrapolation; Audit flagged flipped labels with average precision 0.498 vs 0.451 for a random forest.
They released RealBulk, 1,160 curated public cohorts (194,265 people, 148 disease groups), plus model weights, pretraining code, and the benchmark.
summary.why: This is the most systematic benchmark to date of tabular in-context learning applied to clinical transcriptomics, with a large curated resource (RealBulk) that can serve as a community test bed. For a transcriptomics/multiomics researcher, PRTS offers a drop-in zero-training predictor including censored survival, though the honest takeaway is that it matches rather than clearly beats strong tabular models, and cross-cohort transfer remains the open problem.
summary.limitations: The advantage over TabPFN v3.5 is narrow, partly depends on within-cohort/site structure, and does not survive adjustment against post hoc TabPFN configurations on RealBulk; no ablations of the prior, gene codes, or heads were performed. Cohort linkage was imperfect (34 held-out cohorts linked to development cohorts via an audit), cohorts are retrospective and public, and newer tabular models may close the remaining gap.

also.title: Learning gene co-regulation across cells with Multicellular Transformer
also.abstract: Understanding how genes coordinate across cells is central to explaining tissue function and disease, yet most existing models still take a single cell as input and therefore emphasize cell-intrinsic regulation. We present the Multicellular Transformer (MCT), a foundation model built around a different assumption: cells function together within tissues, so the appropriate unit of input is not one cell in isolation but a set of cells from the same sample. By jointly modeling multiple cells, MCT learns context-aware gene embeddings that capture gene-gene interactions across the tissue environment. Trained on a large set of tissue samples (>4200) across more than 30 tissue types, MCT recovers ligand-receptor interactions, infers cross-cell signaling programs, and reveals spatial co-localization patterns directly from scRNA-seq data. Its contextual embeddings identify disease-specific rewiring of gene neighborhoods in systemic lupus erythematosus and COVID-19 and predict population-level perturbation effects in cancer without additional training. By linking gene-level regulation to tissue-scale organization, MCT provides a scalable framework for modeling multicellular biology and enables in silico discovery of therapeutic targets and tissue-specific dependencies.

summary.tldr: Multicellular Transformer (MCT) is a scRNA-seq foundation model that takes a whole sample (set of cells), not one cell, as input, producing context-aware gene embeddings that capture cross-cell co-regulation, ligand-receptor interactions, and spatial co-localization.
summary.background: Existing single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, scPRINT) take one cell at a time, so their gene embeddings reflect cell-intrinsic regulation and miss tissue-level coordination like signaling between cell types. Cross-cell methods (e.g., DIALOGUE, SCENIC) rely on correlation-based modules that scale poorly and don't generalize across heterogeneous tissues.
summary.approach: MCT encodes each gene with a sample-invariant 'gene function' embedding summed with an expression embedding computed (via a shared two-layer FFNN with input units fixed to ~predefined cell types) from that gene's expression across all cells in a sample, then contextualizes gene embeddings with a 12-layer transformer over ~60k genes. Pretraining uses masked gene-identity prediction (15% masking) plus an expression reconstruction loss on a corpus of >14M cells from >3,500 donors across >4,200 samples and >30 tissue types (>300 harmonized cell types), with dynamic cell subsampling for augmentation. Fine-tuned variants are used for lung cancer and glioblastoma atlases and on Xenium spatial data (samples defined as cells within a fixed radius).
findings: Zero-shot ligand-receptor prediction against CellChatDB pairs (cosine similarity of pretrained gene embeddings) reaches AUROC 0.71 vs 0.65 for the second-best model, scGPT, across contact, secreted, and ECM-receptor interaction types.

Integrating gradients attribute known cell types to known pairs (cDC2/monocytes for TLR4-CD14, Tregs for IL2RA-IL2R, tumor cells for MET-HGF), and combining MCT with ESM-C embeddings in an XGBoost model improves receptor-ligand precision; 6 of 70 top-ranked secreted-membrane pairs from lupus data show AlphaFold3 ipTM > 0.5 (e.g., IL1B-IL1R2 at 0.76).

Comparing gene neighborhoods (Jaccard similarity of top-k embedding neighbors) across conditions flags disease-specific rewiring: IFI44 and MX1 for SLE, OAS1 and CD74 for COVID-19; MCT's top-20 SLE genes overlap 40% with Wilcoxon differential-expression hits while also catching genes (OAS2, FTH1, SH3BGRL3) whose neighborhoods shift despite small expression changes.

Zero-shot in silico knockouts at the sample level recover known interacting-gene dependencies, show 30% overlap with top DepMap hits and Pearson r=0.33 (p<1e-10) for the SW 1573 lung cancer line, and distinguish tumor-selective effects from housekeeping genes; high-embedding-similarity gene pairs co-localize in held-out Xenium/Visium data (bivariate Moran's I), and fine-tuning on spatial data strengthens this correlation.
Averaged gene embeddings yield sample-level representations that cluster by tissue/disease and beat PCA baselines on normalized mutual information in 3 of 4 comparisons.
summary.why: It reframes the input unit of transcriptomic foundation models from cell to sample, giving gene embeddings that are explicitly context-dependent—relevant if your work spans cell-cell communication, tissue-level multiomics, or microenvironment-aware perturbation modeling. Code (github.com/almaan/mct) and all data are public, and it works on any sample expressing a subset of pretraining genes.
summary.limitations: Pretrained embeddings give interaction potential, not mechanism or direction, and cell-type attribution relies on post-hoc explainability (Integrated Gradients); the fixed cell-type-assigned FFNN inputs constrain generalization to unseen cell types, and public-data biases (coverage, protocols, annotations) may limit transfer to underrepresented tissues.

also.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
also.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

summary.tldr: Calpha attaches a pretrained SimpleFold-3B flow-matching structure head to the Qwen3.5-9B LLM so the model can emit a folding trigger token and generate single-chain protein coordinates from its own residue hidden states.
summary.background: Protein structure predictors and general-purpose LLMs are separate: specialist folders like AlphaFold/ESMFold/SimpleFold can't follow instructions or reason in text, while LLMs asked to output coordinates without tools score near random (TM 0.147-0.224 vs 0.138-0.149 random walk). The goal is one native model where language reasoning could eventually influence structure prediction, and the hard first step is whether folding accuracy survives when the structure head is conditioned only through the LLM's hidden states.
summary.approach: Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence with frozen ESM2-3B per-residue features added to amino-acid token embeddings; on a folding request it emits a <structure> token, and an 8.4M-parameter front-end (softmax mixture over 9 Qwen layers) conditions a frozen SimpleFold-3B head (flow matching, 200 sampling steps). Training has two stages: stage 1 jointly trains Qwen (~9B params), the ESM2 adapter, and a 100M SimpleFold head for 2B tokens on 84,658 PDB chains (75% protein tasks / 25% text); stage 2 freezes Qwen and the 3B head and trains only the 8.4M front-end for 30k steps (~11 hours on 8 H200s). All evaluation is on C-alpha atoms via TM-score against FoldBench-334, 155 CASP16 domains, and 200 CAMEO-style 2025 PDB chains.
findings: Calpha reaches mean TM-scores of 0.808 (FoldBench-334), 0.635 (CASP16), and 0.900 (CAMEO-2025), beating ESM3-open, DPLM-2, and token-based variants but trailing ESMFold, SimpleFold-3B public weights, and their own ESM2→SimpleFold-3B direct baseline (0.822/0.682/0.917).

Versus the ESM2→SimpleFold-3B baseline, paired differences are within noise for chains of 100-299 residues but significantly negative at 300-600 residues (mean deltas -0.044, -0.160, -0.025 on the three sets).
Four of five English folding phrasings triggered structure generation on 100% of eligible examples (fifth: 95.5-98.2%), with 0-1.4% false triggers on non-folding protein questions.

Protein training dropped MMLU-Pro accuracy on a 350-item five-shot subset from 77.4% to 70.3% (-7.1 points), and cutting general data share from 25% to 15% cost another ~5 points with no folding gain.

Development ablations show pretrained SimpleFold weights are essential (randomly initialized head: TM 0.270), unfreezing the 3B head hurts, and sample-agreement among 16 draws correlates strongly with true TM (Spearman 0.85-0.89).
summary.why: This is an early proof that structure generation can live inside a general LLM rather than a separate tool, which is the prerequisite for the field's larger goal of language reasoning steering structure predictions (e.g., complexes, bound states). For multiomics/sequence-model researchers, the main lesson is negative but useful: routing folding signals through an LLM currently costs accuracy on longer chains and general reasoning ability, so the interface overhead is not yet paid for.
summary.limitations: Only single chains, C-alpha-only scoring, and one fixed request template are evaluated; complex prediction, structure understanding, side-chain quality, and whether language context actually changes predicted coordinates remain untested, and the long-chain comparison is confounded by differences in training schedule, trainable weights, and crop length.

also.title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
also.abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.
